reference_title: Standard Practice Manual for Flexible Pavements

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: RMP (resin modified pavement) is a tough, durable surfacing that combines HMA flexibility with the fuel, abrasion, and wear resistance of PCC. It is an open-graded AC mixture with 25-35 percent voids filled with a resin modified Portland cement grout, produced and placed separately as a 50 mm (2 in.) thick support layer.
sections.body: RMP is a tough and durable surfacing material that combines the flexible characteristics of HMA with the fuel, abrasion, and wear resistance of PCC, categorized between these two common paving materials. RMP is basically an open-graded AC mixture containing 25 to 35 percent voids that are filled with a resin modified Portland cement grout. The open-graded asphalt mixture and resin modified cement grout are produced and placed separately, and the production/mixture requirements for both differ slightly from conventional procedures. The open-graded asphalt mixture is the support layer and sets the RMP thickness at 50 millimeters (2 inches). It is placed with standard AC paving equipment but is not compacted; compaction would decrease the voids and hinder grout penetration. After placement the open-graded material is simply smoothed with a steel-wheel roller of 3 metric tons (3 tons) maximum. Once the asphalt mixture has cooled, the cement grout is poured onto it and squeegeed over the surface, then vibrated into the voids with the steel-wheel roller until all voids are filled with grout, which essentially completes construction. RMP was developed in France in the 1960s as a fuel- and abrasion-resistant surfacing material (the Salviacim process, developed by the French construction company Jean Lefebvre Enterprises) as a cost-effective alternative to PCC. It has been used on warehouse floors, tank hardstands and roads, and aircraft parking aprons, and is best suited to pavements subjected to abrasive traffic, heavy static point loads, heavy fuel spillage, and channelized traffic. RMP has been constructed successfully in France, Great Britain, South Africa, Japan, Australia, Saudi Arabia, and the United States.
key_points: RMP is an open-graded AC mixture (25-35 percent voids) filled with resin modified Portland cement grout, produced and placed separately.
The open-graded asphalt mixture is the support layer and sets RMP thickness at 50 mm (2 in.); it is placed but NOT compacted.
Grout is poured onto the cooled open-graded mixture, squeegeed, then vibrated into the voids with a steel-wheel roller until fully penetrated.
Developed in France in the 1960s (Salviacim process, Jean Lefebvre Enterprises) as a cost-effective PCC alternative.
Best suited for abrasive traffic, heavy static point loads, heavy fuel spillage, and channelized traffic (warehouse floors, hardstands, parking aprons).
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting RMP as a surfacing alternative between conventional AC and PCC for pavements subject to abrasive traffic, heavy static point loads, fuel spillage, or channelized traffic.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Introduces the two material systems used to build RMP: the open-graded asphalt mixture (Section 7-2.1, covering aggregates and asphalt cement) and the resin modified cement slurry grout (Section 7-2.2, covering aggregate, filler, cement, and the cross polymer resin additive). Each is produced under its own requirements before being combined in the field.
key_points: RMP materials split into two independently produced systems: open-graded asphalt mixture (7-2.1) and cement slurry grout (7-2.2).
Production and mixture requirements for each differ slightly from conventional AC or grout practice.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting or specifying the aggregate, asphalt, and grout materials for an RMP project.

sections.title: Open-Graded Asphalt Mixture
sections.summary: Covers the two material components of the open-graded asphalt mixture portion of RMP: the aggregates (Section 7-2.1.1, gradation and physical properties) and the asphalt cement binder (Section 7-2.1.2).
key_points: Open-graded asphalt mixture materials are the aggregate (7-2.1.1) and the asphalt cement binder (7-2.1.2).
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying materials for the open-graded asphalt support layer of RMP.

sections.title: Aggregates
sections.summary: Required aggregate physical properties (LA abrasion, percent fractured faces, percent flat and elongated) and gradation limits for the open-graded asphalt portion of RMP are given in Table 7-1 and Table 7-2, respectively. The open gradation runs from 100 percent passing the 19 mm (3/4 in.) sieve down to 1-3 percent passing the 75 micrometer (No. 200) sieve.
sections.body: The required aggregate physical properties and the gradation limits for aggregates in the open-graded asphalt portion of RMP are listed in Table 7-1 and Table 7-2, respectively. Table 7-1 requires LA Abrasion (ASTM C131) less than 40 percent; percent fractured faces greater than 70 percent both on material retained (+4.75 mm/No. 4) and passing (-4.75 mm/No. 4) that sieve; and percent flat and elongated particles (ASTM D4791) less than 8 percent. Table 7-2 specifies the open gradation: 100 percent passing 19 mm (3/4 in.); 54-76 percent passing 12.5 mm (1/2 in.); 38-60 percent passing 9.5 mm (3/8 in.); 10-26 percent passing 4.75 mm (No. 4); 8-16 percent passing 2.36 mm (No. 8); 4-10 percent passing 600 micrometer (No. 30); and 1-3 percent passing 75 micrometer (No. 200).
key_points: Table 7-1 Aggregate Physical Properties: LA Abrasion < 40 percent; fractured faces > 70 percent (both +No. 4 and -No. 4); flat & elongated < 8 percent (ASTM D4791).
Table 7-2 Gradation Limits for Open-Graded Asphalt Mixture: 100 percent passing 19 mm (3/4 in.) down to 1-3 percent passing 75 micrometer (No. 200).
The open gradation (25-35 percent design voids) is what allows the subsequent cement grout to penetrate and fill the mixture.
tables: Table 7-2 - Gradation Limits for Open-Graded Asphalt Mixture
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting/qualifying aggregate for the open-graded asphalt mixture portion of RMP.

sections.title: Asphalt Cement
sections.summary: The asphalt cement used in the open-graded mixture is of the same grade normally used in the area; the stiffest (highest viscosity) asphalt cement available is preferred to provide a stable surface for subsequent grouting, meeting ASTM D946, ASTM D3381, or ASTM D6373/AASHTO M 320.
sections.body: The asphalt cement used is required to be of the same grade as that normally used in the area. When possible, specify the stiffest (highest viscosity) asphalt cement available in that area to assist in providing a stable surface for the subsequent grouting operations. Ensure the asphalt cement meets the requirements of ASTM D946, ASTM D3381, or ASTM D6373/AASHTO M 320.
key_points: Use the asphalt cement grade normally used in the area; specify the stiffest (highest viscosity) available where possible.
A stiffer binder provides a more stable surface for the subsequent grouting operation.
Must meet ASTM D946, ASTM D3381, or ASTM D6373/AASHTO M 320.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the asphalt cement grade for the open-graded asphalt mixture portion of RMP.

sections.title: Cement Slurry Grout
sections.summary: Covers the four material components of the resin modified cement slurry grout: aggregate (7-2.2.1), filler (7-2.2.2), cement (7-2.2.3), and the cross polymer resin additive (7-2.2.4).
key_points: Cement slurry grout materials: silica sand aggregate (7-2.2.1), filler (7-2.2.2), Portland cement (7-2.2.3), and cross polymer resin additive (7-2.2.4).
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying materials for the resin modified cement slurry grout used to fill the open-graded asphalt mixture voids.

sections.title: Aggregate
sections.summary: The cement slurry grout requires silica sand meeting the gradation in Table 7-3 (100 percent passing 1.18 mm/No. 16 down to 0-2 percent passing 75 micrometer/No. 200). Silica sand is specified for its soundness and durability and must meet the same wear/soundness requirements as the open-graded AC aggregate; deviations have caused significant constructability problems in the past.
sections.body: The cement slurry grout requires silica sand meeting the gradation provided in Table 7-3. Silica sand is specified because of its soundness and durability. Ensure the silica sand meets the requirements for wear and soundness specified for the aggregate in the open-graded AC. Deviations from these aggregate requirements have resulted in significant constructability problems in the past. To date, no problems or distresses associated with possible alkali-silica reactivity (ASR) have been reported in any RMP, though no information has been found on investigations of this possible phenomenon.
key_points: Table 7-3 Aggregate Gradation for Slurry Grout: 100 percent passing 1.18 mm (No. 16), 95-100 percent passing 600 micrometer (No. 30), 0-2 percent passing 75 micrometer (No. 200).
Silica sand is specified for soundness/durability and must meet the same wear/soundness requirements as the open-graded AC aggregate.
Deviating from the aggregate requirements has caused significant constructability problems historically.
No ASR (alkali-silica reactivity) distress has been reported in any RMP to date, though the phenomenon has not been specifically investigated.
tables: Table 7-3 - Aggregate Gradation for Slurry Grout
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the silica sand aggregate for the resin modified cement slurry grout.

sections.title: Filler
sections.summary: Filler (material passing the 75 micrometer/No. 200 sieve) is normally already present in the grout aggregate; if additional filler is required it must be a Class F (ASTM C618) fly ash with calcium oxide content limited to 5 percent by weight maximum and a minimum of 95 percent passing the 75 micron (No. 200) sieve.
sections.body: Normally, filler or material passing the 75 micrometer (No. 200) sieve is present in the aggregate used in the cement grout. When additional filler is required, ensure it is a Class F (ASTM C618) fly ash with a limit on the calcium oxide content of 5 percent by weight maximum. Ensure the fly ash has a minimum of 95 percent by weight of material passing the 75 micron (No. 200) sieve.
key_points: Filler passing the 75 micrometer (No. 200) sieve is normally already present in the grout aggregate.
Additional filler, if needed, must be Class F (ASTM C618) fly ash: calcium oxide <= 5 percent by weight, >= 95 percent passing the No. 200 sieve.
sections.applicability: Applies when the grout aggregate does not already provide sufficient filler and supplemental fly ash filler is needed.

sections.title: Cement
sections.summary: Portland cement for the slurry grout must conform to ASTM C150, Type I, II, III, or IV. Type I is common for RMP; the other types are used where moderate to high sulfate resistance or high early strength is required.
sections.body: Ensure the Portland cement used conforms to ASTM C150. Ensure the Portland cement used is Type I, II, III, or IV. Type I cement is commonly used for RMP applications. The other types are used where moderate to high sulfate resistance or high early strength is required.
key_points: Portland cement must conform to ASTM C150, Type I, II, III, or IV.
Type I is the common RMP choice; Types II-IV are used for moderate/high sulfate resistance or high early strength needs.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting the Portland cement type for the resin modified cement slurry grout.

sections.title: Cross Polymer Resin Additive
sections.summary: Cross polymer resin additives are commercially available (see Table B-4 vendor list); a typical composition is five parts water, two parts cross polymer resin of styrene and butadiene, and one part water reducing agent, used as a plasticizing and strengthening agent in the grout.
sections.body: Cross polymer resin additives are available on the commercial market, Table B-4. Typical composition is five parts water, two parts cross polymer resin of styrene and butadiene, and one part water reducing agent. This product is used as a plasticizing and strengthening agent.
key_points: Cross polymer resin additive is commercially available; see the Appendix B vendor list (Table B-4).
Typical composition: 5 parts water, 2 parts styrene-butadiene cross polymer resin, 1 part water reducing agent.
Functions as a plasticizing and strengthening agent in the cement slurry grout.
sections.applicability: Applies when sourcing or proportioning the cross polymer resin additive for the cement slurry grout mix.

sections.title: Mixture Design
sections.summary: Covers mixture design/optimum-content determination for the two RMP components: the open-graded asphalt mixture (7-3.1), using a modified Marshall procedure with a French aggregate-based estimating formula, and the cement grout (7-3.2), proportioned per Table 7-4 and tested for viscosity per Table 7-5.
key_points: Open-graded asphalt mixture design (modified Marshall procedure) is covered in 7-3.1.
Cement grout mixture design (proportioning and viscosity control) is covered in 7-3.2.
sections.applicability: Applies when developing the job-mix formula for either the open-graded asphalt mixture or the cement slurry grout.

sections.title: Open-Graded Asphalt Mixture
sections.summary: The optimum asphalt content for the open-graded mixture is found via a modified Marshall procedure on 152.4 mm (6 in.) diameter samples. An estimated optimum content is first computed from a France-derived formula based on aggregate gradation and specific gravity, then bracketed with five trial asphalt contents; the selected content must keep VTM (voids total mix, computed from a dry-weight/volume/theoretical-specific-gravity formula) within the 25-35 percent range while staying below the point where voids-filled increases sharply.
sections.body: Marshall laboratory samples 152.4 millimeters (6 inches) in diameter by 63.5 millimeters (2.5 inches) in height are produced using the determined JMF aggregate gradation and a series of asphalt contents ranging below and above an estimated optimum asphalt content value. The estimated optimum asphalt content is determined using a procedure developed in France and based on aggregate properties: Optimum asphalt content = 3.25 x alpha x Sigma^0.2, where alpha = 2.65/SG (SG = apparent specific gravity of the combined aggregates), and Sigma (the conventional specific surface area) = 0.21G + 5.4S + 7.2s + 135f, with G = percent retained on the 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve, S = percent passing the No. 4 sieve and retained on the 600 micrometer (No. 30) sieve, s = percent passing the No. 30 sieve and retained on the 75 micrometer (No. 200) sieve, and f = percent passing the No. 200 sieve. For example, if the estimated optimum content is 4.2 percent, the laboratory Marshall evaluation normally uses 3.8, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4, and 4.6 percent. The 152.4-mm-diameter samples are compacted at 121 degrees C (250 degrees F) with a 4.536-kilogram (10-pound) hand hammer, 25 blows on one side, three samples per asphalt content. The resulting average VTM and voids-filled data finalize the optimum asphalt content selection: as asphalt content increases, VTM fluctuates over a small range while voids filled increases slowly until a significant jump indicates asphalt is filling voids rather than coating aggregate -- an undesirable condition that hinders subsequent grout penetration. Select an asphalt content below that voids-filled inflection point and within the 25 to 35 percent VTM range. VTM of laboratory specimens and field cores prior to grouting is calculated as VTM = [100 - (WTair / (Volume x SGT)) x 100], where WTair = dry weight of specimen, Volume = pi/4 x D^2 x H (measured diameter D and height H), and SGT = theoretical specific gravity.
key_points: Optimum asphalt content estimated via a France-derived formula: 3.25 x alpha x Sigma^0.2, alpha = 2.65/SG, Sigma = 0.21G+5.4S+7.2s+135f (G/S/s/f = gradation fractions by sieve range).
Laboratory evaluation brackets the estimate with 5 trial asphalt contents (e.g. 3.8/4.0/4.2/4.4/4.6 percent) on 152.4 mm (6 in.) diameter, 63.5 mm (2.5 in.) tall Marshall samples.
Samples compacted at 121 C (250 F), 4.536 kg (10 lb) hand hammer, 25 blows per side, 3 samples per asphalt content.
Select the asphalt content below the voids-filled inflection point and with VTM within the 25-35 percent design range.
VTM formula: VTM = [100 - (WTair / (Volume x SGT)) x 100], Volume = pi/4 x D^2 x H.
sections.applicability: Applies when developing the job-mix formula and optimum asphalt content for the RMP open-graded asphalt mixture.

sections.title: Cement Grout
sections.summary: The slurry grout JMF uses the proportion ranges in Table 7-4 (silica sand, fly ash, water, Type I cement, cross polymer resin). Samples are dry-mixed, then water is added and blended 5 minutes, then cross polymer resin is added and blended 3 more minutes; viscosity is measured immediately after with a Marsh flow cone, averaged over three batches, and must meet Table 7-5's time-dependent viscosity requirements. Components are adjusted within Table 7-4 tolerances to hit the target viscosity.
sections.body: The slurry grout JMF is developed using the range of properties listed in Table 7-4. The slurry grout samples are prepared in the laboratory by first dry mixing the cement, sand, and fly ash in a blender until thoroughly mixed. Then the specified amount of water is added meeting viscosity requirements, and the grout mixture is blended for 5 minutes. After this 5-minute mixing period, the cross polymer resin additive is added and mixed with the grout for an additional 3 minutes. Immediately after the 3-minute mixing period, the grout is poured into the Marsh flow cone and tested for viscosity. A Marsh cone has dimensions of 155 millimeters (6.2 inches) base inside diameter, tapering over 315 millimeters (12.6 inches) to a tip inside diameter of 10 millimeters (0.4 inch), with a 10-millimeter (0.4-inch) diameter, 60-millimeter (2.4-inch) long neck. Viscosity in seconds is measured for each sample, and three different batches of each blend are tested to obtain an average viscosity value. The requirements for viscosity of the grout are provided in Table 7-5: 8-10 seconds Marsh cone flow time within the first 30 minutes after polymer addition, 9-11 seconds after 30 minutes. The individual components of the grout (Table 7-4: silica sand 16-20 percent, fly ash 16-20 percent, water 22-26 percent, Type I cement 34-40 percent, cross polymer resin 2.5-3.5 percent, all by weight) are adjusted within these tolerances to obtain the desired grout viscosity.
key_points: Table 7-4 mix proportions (percent by weight): silica sand 16-20, fly ash 16-20, water 22-26, Type I cement 34-40, cross polymer resin 2.5-3.5.
Mixing sequence: dry-mix cement/sand/fly ash, add water and blend 5 min, add cross polymer resin and blend 3 more min, then test viscosity immediately.
Viscosity measured with a Marsh flow cone (155 mm/6.2 in. base ID tapering to a 10 mm/0.4 in. tip over 315 mm/12.6 in.), averaged over 3 batches.
Table 7-5 viscosity requirement: 8-10 sec Marsh cone flow time in the first 30 min after polymer addition, 9-11 sec after 30 minutes.
Adjust silica sand/fly ash/water/cement/resin proportions within the Table 7-4 tolerance bands to hit the target viscosity.
tables: Table 7-4 - Resin Modified Cement Slurry Grout Mixture Proportions
sections.applicability: Applies when developing and viscosity-controlling the job-mix formula for the resin modified cement slurry grout.

sections.title: Equipment
sections.summary: The open-graded asphalt mixture is placed, transported, and mixed with the same equipment used for dense-graded AC (sweepers, distributors, pavers, AC plants, transport trucks), except for smaller steel-wheel rollers. Cement slurry grout placement uses transit trucks, vibratory steel-wheel rollers, and hand tools, detailed in 7-4.1 (Rollers) and 7-4.2 (Hand Tools).
sections.body: The equipment used to place, transport, and mix the open-graded asphalt mixture is the same as that used to place dense-graded asphalt mixture, except for smaller steel-wheel rollers. This equipment includes sweepers, distributors, pavers, AC plants, and transport trucks. The equipment used to place the cement slurry grout consists of transit trucks, vibratory steel-wheel rollers, and hand tools.
key_points: Open-graded asphalt mixture equipment mirrors conventional dense-graded AC equipment (sweepers, distributors, pavers, AC plants, transport trucks) except for smaller steel-wheel rollers.
Cement slurry grout placement equipment: transit trucks, vibratory steel-wheel rollers, and hand tools.
sections.applicability: Applies when mobilizing equipment for an RMP construction project.

sections.title: Rollers
sections.summary: Rollers used to seat the open-graded asphalt mixture and vibrate the cement slurry grout into it are 3 metric tons (3 tons) maximum vibratory rollers, run in static mode for seating the asphalt and vibratory mode for grout placement. A minimum of two vibratory rollers must be available on site during grouting in case of breakdown.
sections.body: The rollers used to seat the open-graded asphalt mixture and to vibrate the cement slurry grout into the open-graded mixture are (3 metric tons (3 tons) maximum) vibratory rollers. These rollers are used in the static mode only while seating the open-graded asphalt mixture and in the vibratory mode while placing the cement grout. During placing of the grout, ensure that a minimum of two vibratory rollers are available at the job site in case of breakdowns.
key_points: Rollers: 3 metric tons (3 tons) maximum vibratory rollers.
Static mode only while seating the open-graded asphalt mixture; vibratory mode while placing the cement grout.
A minimum of two vibratory rollers must be on site during grouting as a breakdown contingency.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and staging rollers for RMP asphalt seating and grout vibration operations.

sections.title: Hand Tools
sections.summary: Hand squeegees spread the cement grout over the pavement surface during application and remove excess grout once application is complete. Hand brooms smooth joint texture during grout application and roughen the entire grouted surface texture immediately afterward.
sections.body: Hand squeegees are used to spread the cement grout over the pavement surface during application and to remove excess grout from the pavement surface once the grout application is completed. Hand brooms are used to smooth the texture of the joints during grout application and are used to roughen the texture of the entire grouted pavement surface immediately after the grout application.
key_points: Hand squeegees: spread grout during application and remove excess grout after application.
Hand brooms: smooth joint texture during application, then roughen the entire grouted surface texture immediately after.
sections.applicability: Applies to the hand-tool work supporting cement slurry grout placement and surface finishing.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Covers field placement of both RMP components: the open-graded asphalt mixture (7-5.1) and the cement slurry grout (7-5.2, itself covering mixing/transport, placement/joints/curing, and pre- and post-grouting surface protection).
key_points: Open-graded asphalt mixture placement is covered in 7-5.1.
Cement slurry grout mixing/transport, placement, and pavement-surface covering are covered in 7-5.2.
sections.applicability: Applies to the field construction sequence for an RMP surfacing course.

sections.title: Open-Graded Asphalt Mixture
sections.summary: The open-graded mix is mixed, transported, and placed like dense-graded AC, over a light tack coat. It is not compacted, only seated/smoothed with a 3-metric-ton (3-ton) maximum tandem steel-wheel roller in static (non-vibratory) mode: one seating pass at 71 C (160 F), one finishing pass at 38 C (100 F) to remove roller marks.
sections.body: The open-graded mix is mixed, transported, and placed by the same methods and procedures used to place dense-graded asphalt mixture. A light tack coat of asphalt material is first applied on the existing AC on which the RMP is to be placed. After the mixture has been placed with a standard asphalt paver, the mixture is not compacted but is rolled to seat or smooth the surface. This is accomplished with a (3-metric ton (3-ton) maximum) tandem steel-wheel roller once the freshly placed open-graded asphalt layer has cooled to 71 degrees C (160 degrees F). Only use a vibratory roller of this size when it is operated in the static mode, i.e. vibration turned off. One pass of the roller is usually sufficient for seating. With another single pass, the same or a similar-sized roller is used as a finishing roller to remove roller marks once the asphalt layer has cooled to 38 degrees C (100 degrees F).
key_points: Placed and transported like dense-graded AC, over a light tack coat on the existing AC surface.
NOT compacted -- only seated/smoothed, once cooled to 71 C (160 F), with a 3-metric-ton (3-ton) maximum tandem steel-wheel roller in static mode.
One seating pass is usually sufficient; a finishing pass (same/similar roller) removes roller marks once cooled to 38 C (100 F).
sections.applicability: Applies to placing and seating the open-graded asphalt mixture course prior to grouting.

sections.title: Cement Slurry Grout
sections.summary: Covers mixing/transport of the slurry grout (7-5.2.1), its placement including joint formation and curing (7-5.2.2), and protecting the pavement surface both before and after grouting (7-5.2.3).
key_points: Cement slurry grout: mixing/transport (7-5.2.1), placement/joints/curing (7-5.2.2), surface protection before/after grouting (7-5.2.3).
sections.applicability: Applies to the full field sequence for applying resin modified cement slurry grout to the open-graded asphalt mixture.

sections.title: Mixing and Transport
sections.summary: Slurry grout is mixed in a batch plant, portable mixer, or ready-mix truck, with the cross polymer resin added last, after other ingredients are thoroughly mixed. Add the resin at the batch plant if haul time is under 30 minutes, or at the job site if over 30 minutes. Ready-mix truck loads must be mixed thoroughly (rotating drum at maximum rpm) for at least 10 minutes immediately before application; acceptability is ultimately judged by meeting the Table 7-5 viscosity requirement.
sections.body: The slurry grout is mixed in either a batch plant, portable mixer, or in a ready-mix truck. The cross polymer resin is added to the mixture after all other ingredients have been mixed thoroughly. Generally, add the cross polymer resin to the grout mixture at the batch plant if the haul distance is less than 30 minutes. If the haul distance is greater than 30 minutes, add the cross polymer resin to the grout mixture at the job site. When using ready-mix trucks for transporting slurry grout, mix the grout mixture thoroughly at the job site immediately before application for a minimum of 10 minutes. Thorough mixing is best accomplished by rotating the mixing drum at the maximum allowable revolutions per minute. The final control on the acceptability of the mixing process is the mixing of a consistent grout that meets the viscosity requirements.
key_points: Mixed in a batch plant, portable mixer, or ready-mix truck; cross polymer resin is added last, after other ingredients are thoroughly mixed.
Add resin at the batch plant if haul distance < 30 minutes; at the job site if haul distance > 30 minutes.
Ready-mix truck loads: mix at maximum drum rpm for a minimum of 10 minutes immediately before application.
Final acceptability check is a consistent grout meeting the Table 7-5 viscosity requirements.
sections.applicability: Applies to mixing and hauling the cement slurry grout from batch plant or portable mixer to the paving site.

sections.title: Placement
sections.summary: Grout is applied once the bituminous surface is below 38 C (100 F) and each batch passes the Table 7-5 viscosity check, poured and squeegeed low-side-to-high-side in battened lanes up to 6 m wide at about 10-13 kg per 0.8 sq m per 25 mm of thickness, then vibrated in and excess squeegeed off; joints are reworked for continuous bond and the surface is cured with a membrane-forming compound within about 2 hours.
sections.body: Ensure the surface temperature of the bituminous mixture is less than 38 degrees C (100 degrees F) before the application of grout, using a fog spray of water on hot days if needed (without causing ponding). Test each batch of grout at the job site immediately before placement and use only if it meets the Table 7-5 viscosity requirements. The cement grout is poured over the bituminous mixture from the ready-mix truck by means of a pivoting delivery chute and spread with hand squeegees, applied sufficiently to fill the internal voids: 10 to 13 kilograms (22 to 28 pounds) of mixed slurry grout fills 0.8 square meter (1 square yard) for each 25 millimeters (1 inch) of open-graded asphalt mixture thickness at 25-35 percent VTM. Begin grouting at the lowest side of the sloped cross-section and proceed low to high; slopes up to 2 percent are the practical limit for RMP (up to 5 percent has been placed but requires excess handwork and grout overruns). Place the slurry grout in successive paving lanes up to 6 meters (20 feet) wide, separated by 50 mm x 100 mm (2 in. x 4 in.) wooden battens secured to the surface before grouting; grout in the same direction as the asphalt paving operation. Use the small (3-metric ton (3-ton) maximum) tandem steel-wheel roller in vibratory mode over the grout-covered mixture to promote full penetration, then remove excess grout by squeegeeing once the layer is fully saturated, exposing the rough surface and improving skid resistance. Joints between successive RMP lanes must ensure continuous bond: remove wooden battens as soon as grout is applied to surrounding areas and vibrate/rework the underlying area with additional grout and hand brooms; there are no time restrictions on placing successive grout lanes. Saw cut joints between RMP and adjacent PCC pavement to the full RMP thickness and fill with a joint sealant meeting project specifications. Curing of a new RMP surface uses a light coating of white-pigmented, membrane-forming curing compound, applied while the surface is still damp but without excess moisture, normally within 2 hours of completed grout application, using a pressurized spraying machine with one or two coats totaling 4.5 square meters per liter (183.4 square feet per gallon).
key_points: Surface must be below 38 C (100 F) before grouting; each grout batch is viscosity-tested on site against Table 7-5 before use.
Application rate: about 10-13 kg of grout fills 0.8 sq m (1 sq yd) per 25 mm (1 in.) of open-graded mixture thickness at 25-35 percent VTM.
Work low side to high side of cross-slope; practical slope limit ~2 percent (up to 5 percent with extra handwork/overruns).
Successive paving lanes up to 6 m (20 ft) wide, separated by wooden battens; vibrated in with the small tandem roller until saturated, then excess grout squeegeed off.
Joints vibrated/reworked for continuous bond; PCC-adjacent joints saw cut full depth and sealed; no time limit between successive grout lanes.
Curing: white-pigmented membrane-forming curing compound, 1-2 coats at 4.5 sq m/liter (183.4 sq ft/gal), applied within about 2 hours of grouting.
sections.applicability: Applies to the field placement, jointing, and curing of the resin modified cement slurry grout over the open-graded asphalt mixture.

sections.title: Covering Pavement Surface
sections.summary: Prior to grouting, the open-graded pavement is protected from mud, dirt, windblown debris, and other contamination (e.g. rolled polyethylene sheeting mounted on the paver or a movable bridge). After grouting, the pavement and appurtenances are protected from public and contractor traffic for 14 to 21 days (14 for warm/dry curing, 21 for cool/damp), with rain-protection materials for the edges/surfaces kept available at all times during the critical first 24-48 hours; paving stops and protective covering is applied if rain appears imminent.
sections.body: Prior to grouting: protect the pavement and its appurtenances against contamination from mud, dirt, windblown debris, waterborne material, or any other contamination that enters the void spaces of the open-graded asphalt mixture before grout application, by keeping the site clean and covering the pavement with a protective material such as rolled polyethylene sheeting, mounted on either the paver or a separate movable bridge and unrolled without dragging over the surface. After grouting: protect the pavement and appurtenances against both public traffic and contractor traffic for 14 to 21 days, depending on environmental conditions during curing -- 14 days for warm and dry weather, 21 days for cool and damp weather. To protect against rain before the pavement is sufficiently hardened (the first 24 to 48 hours), materials for protecting the edges and surfaces of the unhardened RMP must be available at all times, using the same protective materials/methods as before grouting. When rain appears imminent, stop all paving operations and cover the hardened RMP surface with protective covering.
key_points: Prior to grouting: protect against mud/dirt/windblown debris/water contamination with rolled polyethylene sheeting via paver or movable bridge.
After grouting: protect from public and contractor traffic for 14 days (warm/dry curing) to 21 days (cool/damp curing).
Rain-protection materials for edges/surfaces must stay available at all times during the critical first 24-48 hours.
Stop paving operations and cover the hardened RMP surface with protective covering when rain appears imminent.
sections.applicability: Applies to protecting the RMP pavement surface from contamination before grouting and from traffic/rain during the curing period after grouting.
